story.title: Correcting a transcript requires remembering what was said elsewhere
paragraphs: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) error correction (AEC) rewrites a recognizer's text output, and some errors cannot be fixed from one sentence. The pronouns 他 (he) and 她 (she) are both pronounced tā; in the paper's Table 1, a report names the volleyball player Zhu Ting, yet a sentence-level corrector writes 他 in the next sentence.

A longer input is the obvious fix, but attention cost grows with length and unrelated sentences add noise. The corrector instead keeps a one-sentence input and retrieves internal representations from a larger context; the recognizer itself is unchanged.

mechanism.title: A memory of decoder states extends local attention
paragraphs: The corrector starts from BART fine-tuned for sentence-level AEC. In one decoder layer, the self-attention queries also search a datastore of attention keys and values from other processed tokens, and a gate mixes the retrieved output with local attention (Figure 1). A gate of about 0.4–0.5 works best; larger values let retrieved context override the current sentence.

Two choices set what the datastore holds. Document context limits retrieval to the current transcript; dataset context adds the other documents of the same split, so at test time it holds only test transcripts. Online mode adds each corrected sentence's states as it goes, so only earlier sentences are searchable; offline mode starts from the finished online store and can also use later sentences.

evidence.title: Retrieved context helps where a longer input hurts
paragraphs: More context is not automatically better: a sliding window of neighboring sentences raises error rates above sentence-level BART on all four datasets, and a dual context encoder helps only slightly on three (Table 2). All four retrieval variants beat BART on every dataset, though by far less than BART's own reduction of the raw WeNet (Mandarin) and fairseq (English) output.

Offline beats online and dataset context beats document context, with one tie on LibriSpeech Other. Shuffling the documents or replacing retrieved entries with random vectors raises error rates, so the gain comes from the retrieved context itself (Table 5). The cost is inference time: with 16 neighbors, decoding takes 1.19× BART's time with a document store and 1.50× with a dataset store (Table 7).

demo.title: Which sentences can the corrector search?
demo.description: The kNN attention layer searches a datastore of attention keys and values from other sentences. Two choices decide what it holds (Section 3.4): online or offline timing, and document or dataset scope. Step through the documents and watch which sentences are searchable while sentence A3 is corrected, and whether the sentence that disambiguates it, from the paper’s Table 1 or Table 4, is among them.
demo.note: Published: the sentences, BART outputs and labels of Table 1 (他 or 她, document context) and Table 4 (管撤 or 贯彻, a sentence from another document). Schematic and illustrative: three test documents of five sentences, processed in parallel one position per step as in Figure 2(a), and the positions of the cue and the target, which the paper does not print; the cue position is reader-set. Computed: which sentences are searchable, from the Section 3.4 rules: online mode stores only sentences already corrected, offline mode starts from the finished online store, document context searches the current document and dataset context every test document. Figure 2 marks the current sentence separately, so it is not counted as context. Measured: AISHELL-1 character error rates (Table 2). The demo shows availability only; it does not run retrieval or the gate that mixes retrieved and local attention (0.4–0.5 works best, Section 5.5).
